title: Introduction to i2b2
text:
i2b2









Fig 1. i2b2 Star Schema







i2b2 is Informatics for Integrating Biology & the Bedside Cohort Discovery System
i2b2 is an NIH-funded National Center for Biomedical Computing (NCBC) based at Partners’ HealthCare System in Boston
Enables investigators to identify potential study cohorts using clinical data resources
Intended for protocol development for grant or IRB submission
Provides access to curated data through a web client
Returns only patient counts

title: Electronic Health Records
text:
Clinical Data Warehouse/ Repository




Why?



EHR is designed to support clinical care and workflows, not necessarily research
EHR data is comprised of data from multiple sources and is not readily usable for downstream analysis, which gives rise to the need for a clinical data warehouse or repository






Clinical Data Warehouse (CDW) is a database that consolidates data from a variety of clinical sources to present a unified view of a single patient
It is optimized for record retrieval and reporting, which can be used for research, quality improvement, and operational purposes
Typically, CDWs include but are not limited to data elements like patient demographics, diagnoses, procedures, medications, laboratory results, and vital signs

title: Structured Query Language (SQL)
text:
What is SQL?

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for talking to a relational database, a database that stores data in tables of rows and columns
It’s declarative: you describe what data you want, and the database engine figures out how to retrieve it
Every clinical data warehouse you’ll touch (OMOP, EHR extracts, REDCap exports loaded into a DB) is queried with SQL
In this class we’ll use DuckDB, an embedded, in-process SQL engine: no server to install or connect to, it just runs inside R/Python (or standalone) and can query files directly

title: Structured Query Language (SQL)
text:
Core Building Blocks

Table: a collection of records for one type of entity (e.g. person, condition_occurrence), organized into rows (records) and columns (attributes)
Primary key: a column (or set of columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a table (e.g. person_id)
Foreign key: a column in one table that points to the primary key of another table, letting SQL join related tables together
A query is a statement written in SQL that asks the database a question and returns a table as the answer
In DuckDB, a “table” can even be a CSV or Parquet file queried directly, with no separate load step:

SELECT *
FROM 'condition_occurrence.parquet'
LIMIT 10;

title: Structured Query Language (SQL)
section: What Can You Do with SQL?
text:
What Can You Do with SQL?



These four operations are often called CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete




SELECT: retrieve (read) data from one or more tables (what we’ll focus on in this class)
INSERT: add new rows to a table
UPDATE: modify existing rows
DELETE: remove rows
SQL also lets you filter (WHERE), combine tables (JOIN), aggregate (GROUP BY, COUNT, AVG), and sort (ORDER BY) results:

SELECT gender_concept_id, COUNT(*) AS n_patients
FROM person
GROUP BY gender_concept_id
ORDER BY n_patients DESC;

title: Structured Query Language (SQL)
text:
DuckDB

Embedded, in-process OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) database and needs no server to manage
Reads Parquet/CSV natively, fast on analytic (columnar) workloads
Speaks standard SQL, integrates directly with Python/Pandas/Arrow

Reference : https://duckdb.org/

title: Structured Query Language (SQL)
text:
Connecting to DuckDB


Connect to a persistent OMOP database file

import duckdb
con = duckdb.connect("omop.duckdb")

Run a query and get a Pandas DataFrame back

df = con.execute("SELECT * FROM person LIMIT 5").fetchdf()
print(df)

Use the Relational API style

con.sql("SELECT * FROM person LIMIT 5").show()

Close the connection when done

con.close()

title: OMOP Common Data Model
text:
OMOP Common Data Model




The Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model (CDM) is an open community data standard, designed to standardize the structure and content of observational data and to enable efficient analyses that can produce reliable evidence

title: OMOP Common Data Model
text:
OMOP Common Data Model

The OMOP Common Data Model organizes data into clinical event tables (facts about a patient over time), a person/demographic table, and standardized vocabulary tables
Every clinical fact is represented using a standard concept, which is why most columns end in _concept_id and resolve through concept

title: OMOP Common Data Model
text:
person



One row per patient, this is the anchor table every other table joins back to via person_id










Column
Description




person_id
Unique patient identifier (primary key)


gender_concept_id
Standard concept for sex/gender


year_of_birth, month_of_birth, day_of_birth
Birth date components


race_concept_id, ethnicity_concept_id
Standard demographic concepts


location_id
FK to location (address/geography)


provider_id
FK to provider (usual care provider)


care_site_id
FK to care_site (usual site of care)

title: OMOP Common Data Model
text:
observation_period



Defines the span(s) of time during which a patient’s data is considered complete/observable. Critical for cohort eligibility and lookback/washout logic.










Column
Description




observation_period_id
Primary key


person_id
FK to person


observation_period_start_date
Start of observable window


observation_period_end_date
End of observable window


period_type_concept_id
How the period was derived (e.g., from EHR, insurance enrollment)

title: OMOP Common Data Model
text:
visit_occurrence



One row per patient encounter (inpatient stay, outpatient visit, ER visit, etc.). Most clinical event tables optionally link back to the visit during which they occurred.










Column
Description




visit_occurrence_id
Primary key


person_id
FK to person


visit_concept_id
Type of visit (inpatient, outpatient, ER, etc.)


visit_start_date / visit_end_date
Encounter start/end


visit_type_concept_id
Provenance of the visit record


care_site_id
FK to care_site


admitted_from_concept_id, discharged_to_concept_id
Admission/discharge disposition

title: OMOP Common Data Model
text:
condition_occurrence



Diagnoses - problems, complaints, and clinical impressions recorded for a patient.










Column
Description




condition_occurrence_id
Primary key


person_id
FK to person


condition_concept_id
Standard concept for the diagnosis (joins to concept)


condition_start_date / condition_end_date
Onset/resolution dates


condition_type_concept_id
Provenance (e.g., primary diagnosis, billing code)


visit_occurrence_id
FK to the visit during which it was recorded


condition_status_concept_id
e.g., admitting vs. final diagnosis

title: OMOP Common Data Model
text:
drug_exposure



Records of drug utilization - prescriptions, administrations, and dispensations.










Column
Description




drug_exposure_id
Primary key


person_id
FK to person


drug_concept_id
Standard concept for the drug (joins to concept, typically RxNorm)


drug_exposure_start_date / drug_exposure_end_date
Exposure window


quantity, days_supply, refills
Dosing/supply details


route_concept_id
Route of administration


visit_occurrence_id
FK to the visit during which it was prescribed/administered

title: OMOP Common Data Model
text:
measurement



Quantitative and qualitative clinical measurements - labs, vitals, and other structured test results.










Column
Description




measurement_id
Primary key


person_id
FK to person


measurement_concept_id
Standard concept for the test (joins to concept, typically LOINC)


measurement_date / measurement_datetime
When the measurement was taken


value_as_number
Numeric result (e.g., lab value)


value_as_concept_id
Coded result, when the value isn’t numeric


unit_concept_id
Unit of measure


range_low, range_high
Reference range for the test

title: OMOP Common Data Model
text:
procedure_occurrence



Records of procedures performed - surgeries, imaging, therapeutic interventions.






Column
Description




procedure_occurrence_id
Primary key


person_id
FK to person


procedure_concept_id
Standard concept for the procedure


procedure_date
When the procedure occurred


visit_occurrence_id
FK to the associated visit

title: OMOP Common Data Model
text:
observation



A catch-all clinical fact table for observations that don’t fit condition/drug/procedure/measurement - e.g., family history, social history, survey responses.










Column
Description




observation_id
Primary key


person_id
FK to person


observation_concept_id
Standard concept for what was observed


observation_date
Date of the observation


value_as_number, value_as_string, value_as_concept_id
Result, in whichever form applies

title: OMOP Common Data Model
text:
concept



The vocabulary backbone of OMOP (Standardized Vocabulary). Every *_concept_id column across every table is a foreign key into this table.










Column
Description




concept_id
Primary key - the number stored in every event table


concept_name
Human-readable name


domain_id
Which clinical area it belongs to (Condition, Drug, Measurement, etc.)


vocabulary_id
Source vocabulary (SNOMED, RxNorm, LOINC, ICD10CM, etc.)


concept_class_id
Finer-grained classification within the vocabulary


standard_concept
'S' if this is the standard concept to use for analysis


concept_code
The original code within its source vocabulary

title: OMOP Common Data Model
text:
Standard Concepts

OMOP maps heterogeneous source codes (ICD-10, local lab codes, etc.) onto a single standard vocabulary per domain, so analytic queries only need to filter on standard concept_id values
The concept_relationship and concept_ancestor tables support mapping between source and standard, and traversing concept hierarchies (e.g., “all descendants of Type 2 Diabetes”)

title: OMOP Common Data Model
text:
Connectivity of OMOP Tables



Every clinical event table has a person_id (who) and usually a visit_occurrence_id (during which visit), and every *_concept_id resolves through concept (what, in standardized concept term)

title: SQL Basics
text:
Learning SQL with OMOP


Every OMOP extract uses the same tables and column names, so a query written here can run for any OMOP dataset at any insitution.

Clinical facts live in event tables
Their meaning lives in concept, the vocabulary table

Most of the queries that we will see, you will -

filter an event table,
join to person,
join to concept to get readable names







erDiagram
    PERSON ||--o{ VISIT_OCCURRENCE : has
    PERSON ||--o{ CONDITION_OCCURRENCE : has
    PERSON ||--o{ DRUG_EXPOSURE : has
    PERSON ||--o{ MEASUREMENT : has
    VISIT_OCCURRENCE ||--o{ CONDITION_OCCURRENCE : "recorded during"
    CONCEPT ||--o{ CONDITION_OCCURRENCE : "condition_concept_id"
    CONCEPT ||--o{ DRUG_EXPOSURE : "drug_concept_id"
    CONCEPT ||--o{ MEASUREMENT : "measurement_concept_id"
    PERSON {
        int person_id PK
        int gender_concept_id FK
        int year_of_birth
    }
    CONDITION_OCCURRENCE {
        int person_id FK
        int condition_concept_id FK
        date condition_start_date
    }
    CONCEPT {
        int concept_id PK
        string concept_name
        string domain_id
    }

title: SQL Basics
text:
The dataset




A synthetic OMOP CDM subset stored in a DuckDB database file, omop.duckdb 
Concept IDs are real standard concepts (SNOMED, RxNorm, LOINC)
People, dates and values are simulated
Every chart and table in this deck is a live query against it

title: SQL Basics
text:
SQL Query Syntax

  
  How you write it
  How the database runs it
  
  
    SELECT
    FROM
    JOIN … ON
    WHERE
    GROUP BY
    HAVING
    ORDER BY
    LIMIT
  
  
  
    1  FROM
    2  JOIN … ON
    3  WHERE
    4  GROUP BY
    5  HAVING
    6  SELECT
    7  ORDER BY
    8  LIMIT
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  Aliases are born here,
  so WHERE can’t see them

title: SQL Basics
text:
SELECT and FROM



FROM names the table
SELECT picks the columns you want back
LIMIT keeps the preview small while you explore
Avoid SELECT * in real extracts since OMOP tables are wide, and naming columns documents intent

title: SQL Basics
text:
WHERE filters rows
Move the controls to play with the query. The query text and the result both update





BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends
Filtering on gender_concept_id, not a text label, is the OMOP way

title: SQL Basics
text:
ORDER BY and LIMIT





Without ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed, so LIMIT alone returns an arbitrary sample

title: SQL Basics
text:
JOIN turns IDs into meaning



Event tables store integers
concept holds the names


  
  condition_occurrence

text: INNER, LEFT and ANTI JOINS

title: SQL Basics
text:
GROUP BY does aggregation





COUNT(*) counts records
COUNT(DISTINCT person_id) counts patients

In EHR data these differ a lot

title: SQL Basics
text:
HAVING filters




WHERE runs before grouping, on rows
HAVING runs after grouping, on aggregates


Use this pattern for high utilisers, patients with ≥ 2 diagnosis codes and similar phenotype rules

title: SQL Basics
text:
Dates: Visits over Time




DuckDB
date_trunc('year', d)
SQL Server
DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(d),1,1) OR DATETRUNC(year, d)

title: SQL Basics
text:
Measurements and CASE WHEN





CASE WHEN creates a derived column row by row, which is how most lab-based phenotype flags are built

title: SQL Basics
section: CTEs: build a cohort step by step
text:
CTEs: build a cohort step by step


Question:
Of patients with type 2 diabetes, how many started metformin within N days of diagnosis?


Each WITH block is a named step
Read top to bottom

title: SQL Basics
text:
Beyond the basics
Pattern matching, subqueries, set operations and window functions

title: SQL Basics
text:
LIKE finds concepts by text





% matches any run of characters
_ exactly one





Try %disease, _etformin, %in%, %blood%





Use LIKE to find concept IDs, then filter event tables on the IDs
Text search misses synonyms and is slow on the full vocabulary

title: SQL Basics
text:
String Functions: CONCAT, SPLIT_PART, REGEXP_EXTRACT





|| concatenates
SPLIT_PART and regexp_extract pull pieces out of a string
Source values in OMOP (*_source_value) are free text, so these functions do most of the cleanup.

title: SQL Basics
section: Subqueries: IN, EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
text:
Subqueries: IN, EXISTS and NOT EXISTS


Question:
Which patients have a condition but no record of the usual drug?
This is a classic care gap query





EXISTS stops at the first match, so it never duplicates rows the way a JOIN can
NOT IN breaks if the subquery returns a NULL; prefer NOT EXISTS

title: SQL Basics
text: UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT

title: SQL Basics
text:
NULL-safe summaries: COALESCE, NULLIF, FILTER





race_concept_id = 0 means “no matching concept”, so the LEFT JOIN returns NULL
COALESCE swaps in a label
FILTER (WHERE …) counts a subset inside one group, turning rows into columns
NULLIF(x, 0) returns NULL when x is 0, so a division gives NULL instead of an error

title: SQL Basics
text:
OVER aggregates without collapsing rows




  
  GROUP BY
  
  
  
  
  3
  OVER
  3
  3
  3
  3 visits → 1 row
  3 visits → 3 rows,
  each with the count

title: SQL Basics
text:
ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK





On ties, ROW_NUMBER still counts 1, 2, 3, RANK repeats and then skips, and DENSE_RANK repeats without skipping
ROW_NUMBER() … = 1 is the standard OMOP “first event per person” pattern
DuckDB also lets you write QUALIFY rn = 1 instead of the outer query

title: SQL Basics
section: LEAD and LAG: time between visits
text:
LEAD and LAG: time between visits





LEAD(x) reads the next row’s value in the window and LAG(x) reads the previous one
This is how readmission and gap-in-care measures are built

title: SQL Basics
section: Window frames: running and moving values
text:
Window frames: running and moving values





The frame says which rows around the current one feed the aggregate
ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW gives a 3-reading moving average
With only ORDER BY, the frame runs from the first row, giving a running total or max

Export the result


Pipe-delimited with every field quoted survives commas inside concept names. The year leads the filename so extracts sort by period.
COPY (
  SELECT ...

title: SQL Basics
text:
Recap

FROM which table (and alias) JOIN … ON link tables, usually on person_id or *_concept_id WHERE keep rows, before any grouping GROUP BY collapse rows into groups for COUNT, AVG, MIN HAVING keep groups, after aggregation SELECT choose and compute output columns, incl. CASE WHEN ORDER BY sort, then LIMIT to trim

title: SQL Basics
text:
Recap: beyond the basics

LIKE / ILIKE match text with % and _, to find concept IDs EXISTS keep rows that have (or lack) a related row, without duplicating them UNION · INTERSECT · EXCEPT combine two result sets that have the same columns COALESCE · NULLIF replace NULLs and prevent division by zero FILTER (WHERE …) count a subset inside each group OVER (PARTITION BY …) aggregate per group and keep every row ROW_NUMBER · RANK number rows, e.g. the first event per person LAG · LEAD read the previous or next row, e.g. gaps between visits ROWS BETWEEN … running and moving aggregates
